title: Section 221 — Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content.overview: BNS s. 221 — Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions. BNS restatement of IPC 187. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 187. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 221 is the rule on “Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions”. The section provides that whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 221 exists so that “Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions” has a closed legal test in Chapter XIII — Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Summons, proclamations, false information — and the recast suicide-attempt-to-coerce offence.

The provision in detail
221. Whoever voluntarily obstructs any public servant in the discharge of his public functions, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand and five hundred rupees, or with both

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 221 constitutes a key component of Chapter XIII (Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions under Section 221 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 221.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 221 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 221 vs General Attempt: Section 221 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XIII; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.

Section 221 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 221 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 221 for conduct relating to obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions.
Rule: Under BNS s. 221, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 221.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 221 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
